The shoe decomposition · short report

How much of the post-2017 marathon speed-up is the shoe?

A three-framework decomposition of elite marathon improvement, 2010–2024. Jeremy Lee, May 2026. Updated 28 October 2026: 106 wheelchair and handcycle results the scraper had read as running times are now excluded, which moved the pooled estimate from 67 s to 73 s.

Nike’s Vaporfly 4% went on general sale in 2017, and elite marathon times dropped quickly after it. This report asks how many seconds of that drop the shoe accounts for, using 1,802 elite running performances and three methods that control for different things.

Pooled shoe contribution
73 seconds
95% CI -4 to 150 s · about 1.0% of a 2:05 marathon

The question

Of the elite marathon improvement between the pre-Vaporfly era (2010–2016) and the post-Vaporfly era (2018–2024), how much, in seconds, comes from the shoe? 2017 is a transition year and sits in neither window.

No single method answers that cleanly, so the analysis runs three and compares them.

Framework 1: difference-in-differences

Road marathon improvement minus track 10,000 m improvement over the same window, with the track change rescaled to marathon time. Track racing did not take up carbon plates at the same rate, so anything that sped up both events cancels out.

Framework 2: within-athlete paired

Athletes with at least two elite marathons in each era. Comparing a runner with themselves holds genetics and training history fixed. The race tables carry no ages, so the change is not age-adjusted.

Framework 3: cohort survival

Counts of sub-2:10 (men) and sub-2:25 (women) performances per year, a changepoint search on those counts, and the shift in the top-30 median between eras, of which 55% is attributed to shoes.

The three estimates

Framework 1. Difference-in-differences (road vs track, women-only pre-era)
199 s
[83, 338]
Framework 2. Within-athlete paired (n=16, p=0.39)
44 s
[-62, 121]
Framework 3. Cohort survival (changepoint 2020)
71 s
[58, 98]
Pooled (weighted by inverse squared CI width)
73 s
[-4, 150]

28 October 2026: the bootstrap now resamples the same statistic as the estimate.

Fast times became more common, women’s most of all

The pre-era averaged 23 sub-2:10 men’s performances per year across the major-marathon dataset and the post-era averaged 29, a 1.25× rise. Women under 2:25 went from 13 a year to 25, 2.0×. At the majors the count is capped by the size of the lead packs, so these ratios understate the change across the sport.

Track 10,000 m improved far less

Track times did improve: Cheptegei ran 26:11 in 2020 and Chebet 28:54 in 2024. Across the eras the women’s track numbers moved about 0.3% while the women’s road marathon top-50 median moved about 2.6%. That gap, roughly eight to one, is the main evidence for something road-specific, and the shoe is the most obvious road-specific change. The track control is thin, though: 27 performances, and only 2016 on the pre-era side.

What it adds up to

The shoe accounts for about a minute and a half of elite marathon time, close to 1%, with a wide interval. That is well short of the 4% running-economy gain measured on a treadmill (Hoogkamer et al. 2018). Running economy is not race time: at elite marathon pace an economy gain buys about two-thirds as much speed (Kipp et al. 2019). Deeper East African fields, pace-controlled races and altitude training also changed over the same years. The shoe gets most of the credit in public argument partly because it has a release date.

Limits

  • The track control has 27 rows, and its pre-era side is one year of women’s results. Framework 1 is the weakest of the three for that reason.
  • The within-athlete sample is 16 runners and the paired t-test is not significant (p = 0.39).
  • The 55% shoe share in Framework 3 is a modeling choice, not an estimate.
  • Era stands in for shoe use. Nobody’s footwear is recorded per race.

Reproduce

git clone https://github.com/lyhjeremy/marathon-shoe-revolution-decomposition.git
cd marathon-shoe-revolution-decomposition
pip install -r requirements.txt
python src/analysis.py

Under a minute on an M1 MacBook. The PDF report has the sensitivity analysis and full limitations; the notebook in notebooks/ reproduces every number cell by cell.
